title: Every Day
author: Five Twelve Thirteen
summary: In this practitioner essay, a fifth-grade teacher lays out an 'every day' framework for literacy instruction: eight recurring elements (vocabulary, background knowledge, teacher read-aloud, student read-aloud, discussion, sentence-level writing, close reading, and social studies) that should show up in some form every single day rather than being sequenced by a curriculum's chapter structure. The author argues that skilled reading develops through the synergy of many interwoven skills, not through mastering one skill at a time, and that daily distributed practice across these strands, anchored to a shared content topic, builds proficiency more reliably than isolated skill blocks. The piece is explicit that the specific list is calibrated to the author's own students (below-benchmark oral reading fluency, fifth grade, 90 minutes of literacy time) and should be adapted by grade, instructional time, and assessment data rather than copied wholesale. The essay closes by wondering whether a similar 'every day' model, organized around strands like fact fluency and word problems, could be built for math instruction.
points: Build literacy instruction around eight recurring daily elements (vocabulary, background knowledge, read-aloud, student read-aloud, discussion, sentence-level writing, close reading, and social studies) rather than a single curriculum sequence.
Anchor each day's skills to one shared content topic so vocabulary, writing, and background knowledge reinforce each other instead of functioning as isolated exercises.
Use short, structured sentence-level writing tasks so every student writes successfully every day, not just once a lesson is 'finished.'
Tailor the 'every day' list to your students' assessed skill gaps (e.g., oral reading fluency data) rather than applying a universal list to every grade.
Consider adapting the 'every day' habit-stacking approach to math instruction, organizing strands like fact fluency and word problems the way literacy strands are organized.
quotes: The point here is that skilled reading comes from the synergy of many different skills that are developed in parallel and interconnected.
Learning to read is a slow, steady grind, making progress along different strands while weaving them together. That's my north star: a bit of progress every day.
Reading aloud to students helps them focus more on the meaning of the text and less on decoding, and it models fluency and prosody for students.
We don’t read to say we read something. We talk about what we read. We analyze, we make predictions, we ask questions, we try to understand what the author is saying and why.
The eight elements I described above aren’t universal for all literacy teachers. They depend on the age of your students and the data you collect on their skills.
